title: Basic alarm system
desc: Motion sensor triggers buzzer & LED alarm
content_html:
Materials

  • 1 x Arduino Uno R3 (Nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x PIR Motion Sensor Module (HC-SR501) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Active Buzzer Module (5V) (Nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Red LED (5mm) (Nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Green LED (5mm) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 2 x 220 ohm Resistors (for LEDs) (Nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Breadboard (830 tie points) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Push Button (for arming/disarming the alarm) (Nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x 10k ohm Resistor (for push button pull-down) (Nerokas.co.ke)
  • Male-to-Male Jumper Wires (pack of at least 15) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x USB Cable (Type A to Type B) for Arduino Uno (Nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x 9V Battery with Arduino Barrel Connector (optional, for portable demo) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)

How It Works

Imagine you have a security guard whose only job is to watch a room and shout if someone walks in who shouldn't be there. In this project, our "guard" is a small sensor called a PIR (Passive Infrared) sensor. This sensor can detect the invisible heat that all living things give off. When a warm body (like a person) moves in front of it, the sensor notices the change in heat and sends a signal to the Arduino saying "Something moved!"

The Arduino is like the guard's brain. It is constantly checking the PIR sensor's signal, over and over, many times per second. This is called polling — repeatedly asking "did anything change yet?" When the Arduino sees the "motion detected" signal, it makes a decision in the code (this is called a conditional — an "if this happens, then do that" instruction) and reacts by turning on a red LED and sounding a buzzer, just like a real alarm.

We also add a push button that acts as a key switch — pressing it once "arms" the alarm (turns it on and ready), and pressing it again "disarms" it (turns it off), just like you would with a real house alarm keypad. A green LED shows when the system is safely armed and watching.

This project combines three important ideas: sensing (the PIR detecting motion), decision-making (the Arduino code deciding what to do with that information), and output (the buzzer and LEDs reacting). This is exactly how real-world security systems, streetlights, and even automatic doors work.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Lay the breadboard flat on the table and place the Arduino next to it, not touching.
  2. Insert the PIR sensor's three pins into the breadboard (or connect directly with jumper wires if it has a pin header cable). Identify the VCC, OUT, and GND pins — they are usually labelled on the small circuit board.
  3. Connect the PIR sensor's VCC pin to the Arduino's 5V pin using a jumper wire.
  4. Connect the PIR sensor's GND pin to the Arduino's GND pin using a jumper wire.
  5. Connect the PIR sensor's OUT pin to Arduino digital pin 2 using a jumper wire.
  6. Place the red LED on the breadboard. Connect its longer leg (anode) through a 220 ohm resistor to Arduino digital pin 8. Connect its shorter leg (cathode) to the breadboard's GND rail, then to Arduino GND.
  7. Place the green LED on the breadboard the same way, but connect its resistor-anode side to Arduino digital pin 9. Connect its cathode to GND.
  8. Connect the buzzer's positive pin to Arduino digital pin 7, and its negative pin to GND.
  9. Set up the push button: connect one leg to Arduino digital pin 4, and the same leg through a 10k ohm resistor to GND (this is the pull-down resistor, keeping the reading steady when the button is not pressed). Connect the opposite leg of the button to 5V.
  10. Double-check all GND connections are shared on a common rail — a loose ground wire is the most common wiring mistake.
  11. Connect the Arduino to the computer with the USB cable and open the Arduino IDE.
  12. Type or paste the code from the Full Code section below, then upload it to the Arduino.
  13. Open the Serial Monitor (set to 9600 baud) to watch status messages as you test the system.
  14. Press the push button once. Observe the green LED turn on — this means the alarm is now "armed."
  15. Wait about 15-20 seconds without moving — PIR sensors need a short warm-up/calibration time when first powered.
  16. Wave your hand or walk in front of the PIR sensor. Observe the red LED turn on and the buzzer sound — this is the alarm triggering.
  17. Press the push button again to disarm the system. Observe the green LED turn off, and confirm the buzzer stops responding to motion.
  18. Let students take turns arming, triggering, and disarming the system while explaining out loud what they think is happening at each step.

Full Code


// ----- Basic Alarm System -----
// Motion sensor triggers buzzer & LED alarm
// Push button arms/disarms the system

const int pirPin = 2;      // PIR sensor OUTPUT pin
const int buzzerPin = 7;   // Buzzer signal pin
const int redLedPin = 8;   // Red LED = alarm triggered
const int greenLedPin = 9; // Green LED = system armed
const int buttonPin = 4;   // Push button pin

bool systemArmed = false;      // Tracks whether alarm is currently armed
bool lastButtonState = LOW;    // Stores previous button reading to detect a new press
bool alarmTriggered = false;   // Tracks whether alarm is currently sounding

void setup() {
  pinMode(pirPin, INPUT);        // PIR sends HIGH/LOW signal, so it's an input
  pinMode(buzzerPin, OUTPUT);    // We control the buzzer, so it's an output
  pinMode(redLedPin, OUTPUT);    // We control the red LED
  pinMode(greenLedPin, OUTPUT);  // We control the green LED
  pinMode(buttonPin, INPUT);     // Button reading comes into the Arduino

  Serial.begin(9600); // Start Serial communication so we can see debug messages
  Serial.println("System ready. Press button to arm the alarm.");

  delay(15000); // Give the PIR sensor time to calibrate to the room's normal heat levels
  Serial.println("PIR sensor calibrated and ready.");
}

void loop() {
  bool currentButtonState = digitalRead(buttonPin); // Read the button right now

  // Detect a NEW press (button just went from LOW to HIGH)
  if (currentButtonState == HIGH && lastButtonState == LOW) {
    systemArmed = !systemArmed; // Flip the armed status every time button is newly pressed
    Serial.println(systemArmed ? "System ARMED" : "System DISARMED");
    delay(50); // Small delay to avoid reading the same press twice (debounce)
  }

  lastButtonState = currentButtonState; // Save this reading for next loop comparison

  digitalWrite(greenLedPin, systemArmed ? HIGH : LOW); // Green LED shows armed status

  if (systemArmed) {
    int motionDetected = digitalRead(pirPin); // Check what the PIR sensor sees

    if (motionDetected == HIGH) {
      alarmTriggered = true; // Motion found while armed = trigger the alarm
    }

    if (alarmTriggered) {
      digitalWrite(redLedPin, HIGH);   // Turn on red LED
      digitalWrite(buzzerPin, HIGH);   // Turn on buzzer sound
      Serial.println("ALARM! Motion detected!");
    }
  } else {
    // If system is disarmed, make sure alarm outputs are off
    alarmTriggered = false;
    digitalWrite(redLedPin, LOW);
    digitalWrite(buzzerPin, LOW);
  }

  delay(100); // Short pause to keep loop from running too fast and flooding Serial Monitor
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

SymptomLikely CauseFix
Alarm triggers constantly, even with no movementPIR sensor was not given enough calibration/warm-up time, or its sensitivity potentiometer is set too highWait the full 15-20 seconds after power-up before testing; turn the sensitivity dial on the PIR module counter-clockwise slightly
Nothing happens at all — no LEDs, no buzzer, no Serial messagesLoose USB connection or code did not upload successfullyCheck the Arduino IDE for an upload error message; reconnect USB cable; confirm correct board and port are selected
Button press doesn't arm/disarm the system, or arms and disarms randomlyMissing pull-down resistor causing "floating" voltage readings on the button pinConfirm the 10k ohm resistor is correctly wired between the button pin and GND
LEDs stay dim or don't light up fullyLED wired backwards (reversed polarity) or missing/wrong resistor valueFlip the LED around so the longer leg (anode) connects to the resistor/pin side; confirm 220 ohm resistor is used
Buzzer stays silent even though red LED lights upBuzzer wired to wrong pin, or using a passive buzzer that needs a tone() signal instead of HIGH/LOWConfirm buzzer type is "active" (usually has a sticker/dome top); check wiring matches pin 7 in the code
Alarm won't turn off even after disarming with the buttonalarmTriggered variable not resetting because of a logic error in codeConfirm the else block correctly sets alarmTriggered = false when systemArmed is false

Discussion Questions

  • What does the PIR sensor actually detect — is it seeing light, sound, or something else?
  • Why did we need to wait 15-20 seconds before testing the alarm? What might happen if we skipped that wait?
  • What is the purpose of the pull-down resistor on the push button? What do you think would happen if we removed it?
  • Can you think of a real place in your home, school, or neighbourhood where a system like this could actually be useful?
  • If you wanted the alarm to also send a message to someone's phone, what extra parts or ideas do you think you'd need?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add a second buzzer tone pattern (using tone() and noTone()) so the alarm makes a beeping sound instead of a constant tone.
  • Medium: Add a delay so that once armed, the system waits 10 seconds before actually starting to watch for motion (giving the "owner" time to leave the room, like a real house alarm).
  • Hard: Add an LCD screen or use the Serial Monitor to display a live countdown timer, an "entry delay" before the alarm sounds, and a running log of how many times the alarm has been triggered since the Arduino was powered on.
